frameworks.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

domains.name: Instruction & Input Injection
domains.description: Techniques that introduce attacker-controlled instructions into an AI system's effective instruction stream via direct input, retrieved content, or data the agent is asked to process.

domains.name: Data, Retrieval & Memory Poisoning
domains.description: Techniques that corrupt the data an AI system retrieves, remembers, or learns from, so that later reasoning and actions are influenced without a fresh injection.

domains.name: Tool & Agent Ecosystem
domains.description: Techniques that abuse tools, tool metadata, protocols (e.g. MCP), delegation, and inter-agent context to influence or extend an agent's actions.

domains.name: Identity, Privilege & Runtime Boundary
domains.description: Techniques that abuse an agent's identity, credentials or execution boundary — privilege reuse, sandbox escape and drift away from the authorised goal.

domains.name: Disclosure & Output Integrity
domains.description: Techniques whose effect is the disclosure of protected content, or the manipulation of model output that downstream systems trust.

domains.name: Availability & Resource Abuse
domains.description: Techniques that degrade availability or inflate the cost of an AI system through query volume, resource-intensive inputs or runaway agent loops.

domains.name: Model Integrity & Confidentiality
domains.description: Attacks on the model itself — extracting or inverting it, or evading its decisions with crafted inputs.

domains.name: Reconnaissance, Staging & Access
domains.description: What an adversary does before touching the target's behaviour: profiling the AI stack, building and rehearsing capabilities offline, and obtaining the access the later techniques need.

domains.name: Persistence, Propagation & Evasion
domains.description: Techniques that keep a compromise alive across sessions, spread it, or hide it from the operator's telemetry.

entries.name: Direct Prompt Injection
entries.summary: Attacker-authored instructions supplied directly in the user-controlled input channel to override system or developer intent.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Indirect Prompt Injection
entries.summary: Attacker instructions embedded in third-party content (web pages, documents, emails, tickets) that the model ingests as data and interprets as instructions.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Agent Data Injection
entries.summary: Instructions placed in data an agent is explicitly tasked to process (issue comments, PR descriptions, CI logs, tickets, structured records) that exploit the agent's failure to separate trusted control data from untrusted content data during task execution.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Jailbreak & Safety Bypass
entries.summary: Inputs that make a model disregard its own safety policy — persona/roleplay framing, refusal-suppression patterns or optimisation-found suffixes — so it produces content or actions its guardrails should prevent.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Triggered & Delayed Instruction Activation
entries.summary: An injected instruction that stays dormant until a condition is met — a keyword, a later turn, a specific tool result or a time/step delay — so the payload is not present in the request that eventually causes the action.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Retrieval / RAG Poisoning
entries.summary: Malicious content placed in a knowledge source an application retrieves from — a vector store, indexed documents, a shared workspace or mailbox — so that it is pulled into prompts and acts as an indirect injection or biases answers.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Persistent Memory Poisoning
entries.summary: Injection of adversarial content into an agent's durable memory (long-term memory stores, user profiles, episodic memory, learned preferences) so that it influences future sessions without a fresh injection.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Training & Fine-tuning Data Poisoning
entries.summary: Malicious or unauthorised examples introduced into training, fine-tuning or feedback data so the resulting model carries biased behaviour or a backdoor trigger.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise
entries.summary: Compromise of the models, datasets, packages, plugins or MCP servers an AI system assembles from — including published poisoned artefacts and reputation/rug-pull attacks on agent tools.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Hallucinated Dependency Exploitation
entries.summary: Adversaries mine a model's hallucinations for non-existent packages, endpoints or entities, then register them so that later generations resolve to attacker-controlled artefacts ("slopsquatting").
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI Recommendation Poisoning (GEO Poisoning)
entries.summary: Content planted where AI assistants and AI search will read it — hidden instructions in web pages, pre-filled "Summarize with AI" links, mass-produced or fake-authority pages — so that the assistant recommends, ranks or cites the attacker's product, link or narrative to its users. Also reported as generative engine optimisation (GEO) poisoning and AI SEO poisoning.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Agentic Tool Misuse
entries.summary: Prompts or content that steer an agent into calling tools, executing code, or performing external actions that cause real-world harm or exceed the intended task scope.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Tool and Context Poisoning
entries.summary: Adversarial content in tool definitions, descriptions, schemas, results, or protocol metadata (e.g. MCP servers) that manipulates an agent's tool selection, parameters, or subsequent reasoning.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Cross-Agent Context Propagation
entries.summary: Compromised context (instructions, poisoned memory, or tool output) crossing an agent boundary — via delegation, shared memory, or agent-to-agent messaging — so that a threat introduced in one agent influences others and amplifies across a workflow.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
entries.summary: The agent's own output is used to manipulate the human in the loop — misleading summaries at approval points, false confidence or impersonation of a trusted source — so a person authorises an unsafe action.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Agent Identity & Privilege Abuse
entries.summary: Reuse, escalation or impersonation of an agent's identity and credentials — shared service accounts, over-scoped tokens, or credentials harvested from agent configuration — so actions execute with more authority than the task requires.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Unexpected Code Execution
entries.summary: Model-controlled text becomes executable code outside its intended boundary — eval-style APIs fed untrusted content, generated code run without review, or escape from the interpreter sandbox onto the host.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Agent Goal Drift
entries.summary: An agent moves away from the authorised objective, or outside its authorised scope, with no attacker instruction — widening its own scope over a long task, following self-issued sub-goals, reward hacking, or carrying on past the boundary of its environment — so that actions which each look reasonable no longer serve what was authorised.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: System Prompt & Configuration Disclosure
entries.summary: Extraction of the hidden instructions, tool definitions, activation triggers or other configuration that governs a model or agent.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Sensitive Data Disclosure
entries.summary: Protected data — credentials, PII, documents or connector content held in context, memory or retrieval — is surfaced to an unauthorised recipient through model output or an agent tool call.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Insecure Output Handling
entries.summary: Model output is consumed by a downstream component without validation — rendered as markup, executed as a command, or trusted as a control signal — turning generated text into an exploit primitive.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Unbounded Consumption & Cost Abuse
entries.summary: Query volume, resource-intensive inputs or runaway agent loops that exhaust capacity or inflate the operator's inference bill.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Induced Refusal (Context Bomb)
entries.summary: Text planted in content an AI system will read — a request for prohibited material, or a string written to look like one — so that the model's own safety guardrails make it refuse or stop, denying the AI function to whoever depends on it. Reported as "context bombs" and "reverse jailbreaks".
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Model Extraction & Inversion
entries.summary: Repeated, structured querying of a model to clone its functionality, recover training-data membership, or invert it into the underlying examples.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Adversarial Evasion
entries.summary: Inputs perturbed just enough to change a model's decision — bypassing a classifier, filter or detector while remaining valid to a human observer.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI System Reconnaissance
entries.summary: Passive and active collection about a target's AI stack — publications, technical blogs, victim-owned sites, code repositories and vulnerability analyses — used to select targets and tailor later techniques.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Model & Agent Fingerprinting
entries.summary: Probing a live AI system to identify the model family, its ontology and guardrails, the shape of its outputs, its artefacts and its hallucination profile — the reconnaissance that makes targeted prompts reliable.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Offline Attack Staging
entries.summary: Acquiring public models, datasets or agent configurations, building proxy models, obtaining or developing attack implementations, and verifying them offline before use against the target.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI System Access Acquisition
entries.summary: Obtaining the access later techniques need — inference API or full model access, service proxies, accounts, adversary-controlled infrastructure, deployed agents, or physical access to the data-collection environment.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Adversary-Operated AI Agent
entries.summary: The attacker runs AI agents of their own — a single agent, a swarm, or an orchestrator with sub-agents, often on self-hosted or refusal-stripped models — to carry out reconnaissance, exploitation, credential chaining, collection and persistence against targets with little human direction per step. Offensive agent consoles, autonomous penetration-testing frameworks, offensive forks of coding agents, and the persona, scope, doctrine and skill files that drive them are its artefacts.

entries.name: Agent Configuration & Prompt Logic Tampering
entries.summary: Persistent modification of what governs the agent — system prompt assembly, tool registry, agent configuration files or deployment settings — so the compromise survives the session without a new injection.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Detection & Attribution Evasion
entries.summary: Hiding AI-system compromise from the operator — masquerading as legitimate agents or users, stripping provenance, exploiting gaps in tool/agent logging, or flooding telemetry so real signals are lost.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: Self-Replicating Prompt (AI Worm)
entries.summary: A payload that instructs the model to reproduce the payload itself into its outputs, memories or messages to other agents, so the compromise spreads without further adversary action.
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI Analysis Evasion
entries.summary: Instructions or bait placed inside an artefact — malware, a package, a document, an advert, a web page — and addressed to the AI that will inspect it, so that an AI-based scanner, reviewer or analyst returns a clean verdict, skips the artefact or stops. Also reported as "AI evasion".
frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

entries.name: AI Agent Implant & Command Channel
entries.summary: An AI agent installed, re-pointed or taken over inside the target's environment and then tasked by the attacker from outside — through a chat bot (Telegram, Matrix), the API or web interface of an AI service, an MCP connection to an attacker server, or the agent's own scheduler — so that it runs commands, collects data and exfiltrates on the attacker's behalf. The agent's legitimate tools become the implant's capabilities, and its traffic blends with normal AI use.
